To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the longitudinal diffusion coefficient in the mesophyl is much smaller than in the xylemphloem, that the spatial heterogeneity of transpiration rate and the mesophyll tortuousity have a strong effect on the spatial patterns in leaf water isotopes and that these patterns are in steady-state around midday only.

the longitudinal diffusion of isotopes in the mesophyllo is not sufficient to explain the reduction of Delta(lw), that the mesophyll tortuositiy is the most sensitive parameter of the model, and that the Delta(lw) spatial patterns are only in steady state around noon.

the spatial patterns of Delta(lw), which are often assumed to reflect the spatial patterns of gas-exchange parameters, are in fact mainly determined by the mesophyll tortuousity, and that the spatial patterns are in a steady state around mid day, just as the bulk leaf water isotope signal.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the spatial patterns of water isotope enrichment along monocot leaves and the underlying mechanisms that control them.
the spatial and temporal dynamics of water isotopes in plants and their use in ecohydrology.
the spatial patterns of water isotope enrichment along monocot leaves and how these are influenced by leaf anatomy, transpiration rate and its spatial distribution.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the transpiration-driven water enrichment patterns along monocot leaf veins and in their mesophyll are mainly determined by leaf anatomy and gas exchange parameters.
the transpiration-driven spatial pattern of leaf water isotopic enrichment is a complex result of competing effects, and that it is not possible to identify the dominant effect.
spatial patterns of Delta(lw), as measured along the leaf length, reflect the combined influence of leaf anatomy and gas-exchange parameters, which are difficult to separate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the spatial distribution of Delta(lw), and thus of leaf water potential along the leaf, is mainly driven by the leaf geometry and mesophyll tortuousness, and that the non-uniform gas exchange and the non-steady state effects have only a limited impact on Delta(lw).

the spatial patterns of Delta(lw), and their variation between species and conditions, are the result of the interplay between advection, diffusion, leaf length, inter-veinal distance and mesophyll tortuosities, which are all influenced by leaf anatomy and gas exchange.

the spatial patterns of Delta(lw), which are the result of a combination of leaf geometry, leaf anatomy, gas-exchange parameters, non-steady state and diffusion processes, can be well predicted by the model, provided that the model parameter values are known.
The main takeaway from our work is that

spatial patterns of Delta(lw), and their upscaled values, are a good proxy for bulk leaf Delta(w) and can therefore be used to estimate transpiration rate, leaf conductance, and leaf water potential, provided the spatial patterns of gas-exchange parameters are known.

the model is a useful and flexible tool that can be adapted to a wide range of conditions, and that the observed spatial patterns of Delta(lw), which are the result of a complex interplay of several processes, can be easily upsized to the whole leaf.
spatially heterogeneous transpiration rate is a key parameter to explain the spatial patterns of Delta(lw).
